# Install software

- Download and install QGIS from <https://qgis.org/download/>. (3.44 LTR version)
- Download and install R from <https://cran.r-project.org/>
- Download and install RStudio from <https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio>.

# ***Part 1: Explore Image Data in QGIS***

# ***Part 2: Remote sensing analysis and spatial analysis in R***

::: {style="padding: 15px; border: 1px solid transparent; border-color: transparent; margin-bottom: 20px; border-radius: 4px; color: #31708f; background-color: #d9edf7; border-color: #bce8f1;"}
**Goal:** Carry out your first remote sensing analysis and get familiar with R and RStudio. The analysis involves classifying land cover types using the digitized reference data provided in Part 1, while learning basic R syntax and how to work with spatial data.
:::

**Data:** You should also incorporate the digitized land cover type polygons from part 1 of this exercise (refered to as ' *lab1_my.gpkg*' below). The attribute representing the land cover types - Forest, Cropland, Grassland, Settlements, Water, Wetland, and Other land - is named *Type* in the example provide below. Your name of this attribute and the names representing the classes may differ.

## Task 1: Spatial data in R

First read in vector data to be used.

```{r}
library(sf)
g <- read_sf("data/lab1_my.gpkg") #Read your digitized polygons
g$ID <- c(1:nrow(g)) #Create a unique ID for each polygon (record/row)
plot(g["Type"]) #Plot the attribute (Column) containing the land cover types. 
ar5 <- read_sf("data/lab1.gpkg","ar5") #Read the Norwegian land cover dataset AR5 (Arealressurskart 1:5000) 
plot(st_geometry(ar5)) #Plot only the geometry (outline) of this
```

### Making overlay analysis i R - intersection

R can be used to do spatial analysis e.g. overlay anlysis such as union ( *st_union* ), intersection ( *st_intersection*) and more.

```{r}
g <- st_transform(g,st_crs(ar5)) # project coordinat system of your polygons to the same system as ar5 - land cover dataset. 
int <- st_intersection(ar5,g) #If error see below
plot(st_geometry(int))
```

### Geting raster data (optical imagery) into R

There are several packages that allows for getting raster data into R. The most common is the **raster** package that now is gradully replaced by the **terra** package. In addition there is a package called **stars** dealing with spatiotemporal arrays.

```{r}
library(terra) #Load the terra package if you not install you need to install it (install.packages())
# Sentinel 2
s2 <- rast("data/sentinel2A.tif")
plot(s2)
plotRGB(s2, r=3, g=2, b=1, stretch="hist")
```

We like to extract pixels from our training areas and combine them with the interpreted information i.e. your polygons. To extract pixel values for the digitized polygons we used the *extract* function of the **terra** package and combine the two data sources.

```{r}
#If you have a older version you need to convert the sf object into a terra vector data
#g <- vect(g)
e <- extract(s2,g) # Extract information 
head(e)
g2 <- merge(g,e,by="ID") #Merge the two tables into one using ID
g2$Type <- as.factor(g2$Type) # Convert to factor i.e. categorical variable in R
head(g2)
```

## Task 2: Create a classification

We aim to create a classification model using the data extracted from our training polygons. In this example, we employ the randomForest algorithm. Random forests are an easy-to-use machine learning algorithm that usually preforms well.

```{r}
library(randomForest)
rf1 <- randomForest(Type~Blue+Green+Red+NIR,data=g2)
pred <- predict(s2,rf1)
plot(pred)
#writeRaster(pred,"data/lab1/classification.tif") # Save to disk (# means that it is commented out and will not be run, remove # to save on disk)
```

We could also use other classification algorithms, such as linear discriminant analysis (LDA).

```{r}
dat <- st_drop_geometry(g2[,-1])
head(dat)
library(MASS)
lda1 <- lda(Type~.,data=dat)
pd <- function(lda1,..){predict(lda1,..)$class}
pred <- predict(s2,lda1,fun=pd)
plot(pred)
#writeRaster(pred,"data/lab1/classification_planet2.tif")
```

> ***NOTE:*** Any differences? Where are the errors. Can you improve?

## Task 3: Check accuracy

Accuracy is evaluated using a so-called error matrix that summarizes the number of observations according to the actual class and predicted class. The diagonal of the matrix shows the correctly classified observations. A useful reference for the error matrix is: Congalton, R. G. (1991). A review of assessing the accuracy of classifications of remotely sensed data. Remote Sensing of Environment, 37(1), 35–46. [https://doi.org/10.1016/0034-4257(91)90048-B](https://doi.org/10.1016/0034-4257(91)90048-B){.uri}

```{r}
library(dplyr)
pkt <- st_sample(ar5,size=1000) # Random sample of points within the ar5 dataset
pkt <- st_intersection(ar5 %>% dplyr::select(IPCC,geom),pkt) #Intersection with ar5 i.e. extract teh IPCC - value 
head(pkt)
e <- extract(pred,vect(pkt)) #Extract predicted value from the pixel at the point location
pkt <- cbind(pkt,e[,-c(1)]) #Combine 
names(pkt)[2] <- "Predicted"
head(pkt)
pkt$Reference <- substr(pkt$IPCC,1,1)
pkt$Predicted <- factor(pkt$Predicted,labels=unique(pkt$Reference),levels=unique(pkt$Reference))
pkt$Reference <- factor(pkt$Reference,labels=unique(pkt$Reference),levels=unique(pkt$Reference))
#Create errormatrix
em <- xtabs(~Predicted+Reference,data=pkt,addNA=T)
em
sum(diag(em)) / sum(em)
```
